extracted.intended_audience: readers and students of intellectual/moral history; scholars of classical antiquity
extracted.subtask_description: Close-reading and extraction of standards, principles, and characteristic traits of moral thought and social practice in the late Pagan (Roman/Greek/Egyptian) world, as discussed by a 19th-century historian. Focuses on slavery, Stoicism, Cynicism, rhetoricians, religious reformers, and the rise of mysticism.

rubrics_metrics.name: duty_of_humanity_to_slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers (Plato, Aristotle, Zeno, Epicurus, especially Roman Stoics like Seneca) taught that masters have a moral duty of humanity toward slaves — to abstain from cruelty and even from contempt, remembering that position does not affect real human dignity.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Seneca exhorts masters to remember that the accident of position does not affect real dignity; slave may be free by virtue while master may be a slave by vice. This duty is presented as a central ethical obligation repeatedly inculcated by philosophers and echoed in juristic maxims used by judges.

rubrics_metrics.name: legal_reforms_protecting_slaves
rubrics_metrics.description: Imperial legislation progressively limited masters' rights and protected slaves: e.g., Petronian law (forbade condemning slaves to beasts without a judge), Claudius' decrees regarding exposed sick slaves, Nero's appointment of a judge to punish barbarity, and Hadrian's deprivation of the right to kill slaves and other reforms.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Specific statutes and imperial ordinances are cited as concrete measures that improved slaves' legal position — forbidding mutilation, appointing officers to hear complaints, restricting torture to certain witnesses, compelling sale of cruel masters, making emperor's statue an asylum for slaves. These laws are used to support the claim that Imperial slave-code compared favorably with some Christian nations.

rubrics_metrics.name: slave_fidelity_as_moral_evidence
rubrics_metrics.description: The fidelity, courage, and self-sacrifice of many slaves (refusing freedom to avoid betraying masters, accompanying them in flight, rescuing owners at cost of own lives) are presented as a pre-eminent Roman virtue and evidence that masters were not uniformly tyrannical and slaves not uniformly degraded.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites annals of civil wars and Empire crowded with examples of slaves' fidelity; uses such instances to rebut charges of universal tyranny of masters. This functions as a moral-evaluative standard for judging Roman slave society.

rubrics_metrics.name: philosophers_as_moral_directors_and_consolers
rubrics_metrics.description: Philosophers acted publicly as directors of conscience: consolers in bereavement, advisors in perplexing moral cases, popular preachers, and sometimes domestic chaplains entrusted with education and moral discipline.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: They were habitually called in on family bereavement, dying men's comforters, tasked with special exhortations for every vice, and often kept in great families as moral guides. Their methods ranged from private counsel to popular lectures and preaching; they had influence through bedside counsels and public oratory.

rubrics_metrics.name: cynic_monk_ideal
rubrics_metrics.description: The Cynic (described as a 'monk of Stoicism') should devote life wholly to instructing mankind: unmarried, wearing mean dress, sleeping on the ground, living austerely, abstaining from pleasures, preaching publicly without respect or fear, and loving even those who beat him.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Epictetus' dissertation is cited as a picture of the ideal Cynic: mission-like behaviour, itinerant preaching (market-places, highways), complete renunciation of family and comfort, fearless rebuke of vice — presented as both model and example of an ascetic moral career (with parallels to mendicant monasticism).

rubrics_metrics.name: rhetorician_profession_and_its_effects
rubrics_metrics.description: The itinerant rhetorician is characterized as an influential but often superficial public educator: skilled in histrionics, gestures, and polished delivery, sometimes vain and rapacious, cultivating minute artistic parts of oratory, and contributing to popular education and taste while also evidencing decadence of public taste.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Rhetoricians delivered elaborate harangues, personated Homeric characters, eulogized trivial subjects, defended paradoxes, recited prepared harangues or engaged in ready debate; many acquired wealth and public enthusiasm. Their prominence is presented both as a social fact and as symptomatic of cultural decline (vanity, rapacity, frivolity).

rubrics_metrics.name: stoic_principles_of_equality_and_virtue
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoic ethical maxim: 'all men are by nature equal, and virtue alone establishes a difference between them' — the Stoics taught that accident of social position does not alter real human dignity and that virtue is the true measure of worth.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: This principle influenced juristic maxims and legal decisions; it underlies Stoic exhortations to masters about humane conduct toward slaves and was widely borrowed into public law and notions of equity.

rubrics_metrics.name: pedantry_and_retrospective_taste_in_late_scholars
rubrics_metrics.description: Late-antique scholars and literary societies fell into pedantry: minute verbal criticism, obsession with antiquated words and etymologies, preference for obsolete authorities, and amusement in scholastic syllogisms and casuistries — symptomatic of intellectual decadence after the age of genius.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Aulus Gellius' 'Attic Nights' is used as evidence: scholars delighted in trivial grammatical debates, syllogistic amusements, and retrospective adoration of early Republican regulations; author frames this as a shift from originality to fastidious, archaic scholarship.

rubrics_metrics.name: decline_of_stoicism_and_rise_of_mysticism
rubrics_metrics.description: Stoicism's decline is attributed partly to internal decay (casuistry, imposture) but chiefly to a shift of men's minds toward Oriental religions and a mystical, ecstasy-valuing philosophy (Neoplatonism), which appealed by emphasizing emotion, religious yearning, and mystical intuition over Stoic aridity and sceptical subtleties.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author notes the attraction of oriental doctrines (Egyptian, Judaeo-Hellenic syncretism, Gnosticism, Neoplatonism), commerce, slave populations, and Alexandria's intellectual climate. Mysticism offered what Stoicism lacked: emotional religiosity, theurgy, and ascetic practices, leading many away from Stoic ethics.

rubrics_metrics.name: greek_rationalistic_vs_egyptian_mystical_tendencies
rubrics_metrics.description: Two recurring tendencies in religious reform: the Greek (rationalistic, eclectic, allegorising) which judges and refines popular belief, and the Egyptian (mystical, devotional, ritualistic) which emphasizes mystery, initiation, abstinence, and awe — both contributing differently to religious reformation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Greek reform (Plutarch, Maximus of Tyre) applied allegory and moral criticism to purge immoral elements; Egyptian religion contributed ritual, initiation, chastity, and awe. Their fusion (e.g., Neoplatonism, Alexandrian syncretism) prepared the way for later religious developments including Christianity.

rubrics_metrics.name: plutarchs_method_of_religious_reform
rubrics_metrics.description: Plutarch's method combined a defense of reason with acceptance of a supernatural basis to religion: he argued against superstition, applied moral tests to myth, accepted dæmons and a future retribution (not physical torment), and reconciled popular personified divinities with a monotheistic conception by allegory and moral reinterpretation.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Plutarch distinguishes superstition from philosophical religion, rejects immoral fables about the gods, uses allegorical interpretation to 'sublimate' popular worship into harmless symbolism, and accepts intermediate spirits (dæmons) as mediators — an approach the author views as important for preparing Christianity.

rubrics_metrics.name: neoplatonic_ascetic_intuitive_epistemology
rubrics_metrics.description: Neoplatonism privileges intuitive, supersensual reason attained after long discipline (ecstasy/quietism) over discursive reasoning; it is pantheistic in aim to 'bring the God in us into conformity with the God in the universe,' emphasizes subduing the body, denigrates pleasure as the greatest evil, and promotes ascetic morality.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Porphyry and other Neoplatonists are cited: philosophy anticipates death, senses and bodily pleasures are obstacles to divine apprehension, and rigorous discipline is necessary for transcendental intuition. This contrasts with Stoic valorization of active, self-controlled virtue.

rubrics_metrics.name: religious_instinct_and_need_for_positive_belief
rubrics_metrics.description: Human beings possess enduring religious instincts and a desire for positive religious belief; periods of intense scepticism (Epicureanism, Euhemerus-influenced disbelief) are unstable and are followed by revivals of superstition, worship, and religious reform.
rubrics_metrics.guidance: Author cites the social causes (political dissolution of Republic, commerce with East, Oriental slaves in Rome, pestilence) that increased the desire for definite religious belief, leading to revival of Isis/Serapis worship, oracles, and feverish superstition under the Antonines; treats this as a general psychological and historical law.
